```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
# Support rendering from reports/ or from the project root.
project_root <- if (file.exists("data/raw/conflict.csv")) "." else ".."
conflict <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "data/raw/conflict.csv"))
```

I want to describe how the number of distinct recorded conflicts changes over time and assess whether reporting differences could affect the pattern.

## Review of the files and earlier work

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
conflict <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "data/raw/conflict.csv"))
glimpse(conflict)
summary(conflict)
```

I reviewed the README and earlier data-preparation script to refresh my understanding of the project. I selected conflict.csv because it contains conflict identifiers and years, which are needed to count distinct conflicts over time. The earlier script treats best as deaths and applies a 25-death threshold within each country-year-conflict group. However, no codebook was available to confirm the exact meaning of each raw record or the source’s definition of armed conflict.

## Missing values and repeated records
```{r}
conflict |>
  summarise(
    missing_year = sum(is.na(year)),
    missing_id = sum(is.na(conflict_id)),
    repeated_rows = sum(duplicated(conflict))
  )
```

I checked the year and conflict identifier fields for missing values and examined repeated rows. There were no missing years, but 2,696 records had missing conflict identifiers. These records were excluded from the distinct-conflict counts because they could not be assigned to an identifiable conflict. Many rows shared the same recorded values, but these were not necessarily duplicate events. I therefore retained the raw data and prevented repeated records from inflating the counts by counting each conflict identifier only once per year.

## Annual counts and line graph
```{r}
annual <- conflict |>
  filter(!is.na(year), !is.na(conflict_id)) |>
  distinct(year, conflict_id) |>
  count(year, name = "conflicts") |>
  arrange(year)

annual
```

I counted the distinct conflict identifiers recorded in each year. A conflict appearing in multiple records or countries within the same year was counted once. This measures the number of recorded conflict IDs, rather than the number of events, new conflict onsets, or conflicts meeting the earlier 25-death threshold.

```{r}
ggplot(annual, aes(year, conflicts)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Distinct recorded conflicts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

I created a line graph showing annual counts of distinct recorded conflicts from 1999 to 2018. Counts fluctuated during the earlier years, reaching a minimum of 158 in 2010, before generally increasing to a peak of 296 in 2017. The largest annual increase occurred in 2014, when the count rose by 45. These patterns describe the available records; further investigation is needed to determine whether they reflect changes in conflict activity, reporting, or classification.

## Investigating unusual changes and coverage

Find the largest annual change
```{r}
annual |>
  mutate(change = conflicts - lag(conflicts)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(change)))
```

we can observe that the largest annual change occurs
in year 2014 by 45

examine record volume, missing IDs, and represented countries
```{r}
conflict |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    missing_ids = sum(is.na(conflict_id)),
    countries_with_identified_records =
      n_distinct(iso[!is.na(conflict_id)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

I compared annual conflict counts with the number of records, missing conflict identifiers, and countries represented. Between 2011 and 2012, the number of records increased from 7,682 to 18,443, while distinct conflicts increased from 173 to 203. Record volume then declined after 2014, although distinct conflicts continued to increase through 2017. This shows that more records do not necessarily mean more distinct conflicts. Missing identifiers remained relatively stable, and the increases did not consistently coincide with more countries being represented. However, these checks cannot determine whether the changes reflect actual conflict activity or differences in reporting. Source documentation and information about coding changes would be needed to investigate further.

## Observations and next steps

The number of distinct recorded conflicts fluctuated during the earlier years and generally increased after 2010, reaching its highest level in 2017. Counting each conflict identifier once per year prevented repeated records from inflating the totals. However, the available data cannot establish whether these trends reflect changes in conflict activity, reporting coverage, or classification.
My next step would be to obtain the original codebook to confirm what each row represents, how armed conflict is defined, and whether conflict identifiers remain consistent over time. I would also investigate the larger increases in 2012, 2014, and 2017 by examining which identifiers appeared or disappeared and checking for documented changes in reporting or coding.
